children: Nvidia

plunged 14% on Friday and the Nasdaq Composite lost 5.3%, capping the index's worst week since 2020 as investors questioned whether the trillions of dollars being poured into artificial intelligence will pay off. The rout dragged Bitcoin
to its lowest levels since the summer.
The selloff marks the biggest test yet for the AI boom that has driven markets for three years. Analysts are now divided over whether it is a healthy correction or the start of a dot-com-style bust.
The Nasdaq closed at 22,617.73, about 18% below its Oct. 6 record and down 10% for the week, erasing its gains for 2026. The S&P 500 slipped into correction territory.

Nvidia closed at $125.53, down 47.5% from its October record of $239.24, after losing nearly 23% over the week. The chipmaker beat earnings estimates and raised its outlook on Tuesday, but those results have done little to slow the slide following Jensen Huang's departure as CEO.
The losses extended across AI suppliers and infrastructure firms. CoreWeave
closed at $39.51, nearly 80% below its 2025 peak, while Oracle
is down about 70% from its highs. AMD
fell 20.5% for the week, and the iShares Semiconductor ETF
dropped 17.4%.
Newly listed Anthropic
, which raised $81 billion in the largest IPO on record, closed its first day 17% above its $83 offering price before falling about 9% on Friday.

Crypto has been pulled down with tech. Bitcoin ended the week near $58,895, down 9.8% for the week and more than 50% below its 2025 peak, while the total crypto market value fell to about $2.01 trillion, half its peak. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index dropped to 9, signaling extreme fear. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw $582.2 million in net outflows on Thursday.

Some prominent voices see a bubble. Owen Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management, told Fortune he now sees a 70% chance the U.S. stock market is in one, after arguing in January that it was not. Bank of America's November fund manager survey showed investors cutting tech exposure by the most since 2006.

Others see a reset rather than a collapse. Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, called it an "AI repricing" tied to slowing data center construction and tighter funding, Reuters reported. Lawrence Gillum, chief fixed income strategist at LPL Financial, said the decline was "not a bubble bursting."

Prediction markets lean toward more pain. Polymarket traders put the odds of a defined AI industry downturn by year-end at about 54%, though the contract requires several specific events, including Nvidia closing 50% below its record high.

Higher interest rates add pressure. Investors increasingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates again at its Dec. 9 meeting, which would raise financing costs for data centers and hurt stocks whose valuations rest on future profits.
Shares of Nvidia
are currently trading at $125.53.

title: Nvidia Falls 48% From Peak as AI Selloff Spreads to Bitcoin and Crypto
